newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: S. Africa gears up to adopt liberal abortion law.
newsitem.headline: S. Africa gears up to adopt liberal abortion law.

text.p: South Africa's first black-led parliament, overriding howls of protest from a strong Christian lobby, is set to adopt one of the world's most liberal abortion bills.
The bill goes to a vote on Tuesday in the National Assembly and passage is assured by the support of President Nelson Mandela's ruling African National Congress.
The ANC has 252 of the 400 seats in the assembly and, controversially, has denied a free vote, allowing its MPs to follow their individual consciences on the emotive issue.
Legislators preparing the final draft have rejected a public outcry over teenagers who will not have to seek parental consent before undergoing an abortion.

But in a major concession, they have decided that doctors and health workers with a conscientious objection do not have to perform the procedure, nor refer the patient to a facility that will carry out the abortion.

In a country where one can swear on television but never blaspheme, the ANC has been faced with a strong Christian lobby which rejects abortion under any circumstances and advocates celibacy until marriage.

Handing out U.S.-made pink plastic foetuses, home-made chocolate-coloured ones and bloody pictures of terminated foetuses, anti-abortionists have harangued MPs at parliamentary debates and staged protests nationwide.
Health Director General Olive Shisana said she was unruffled by fears, voiced by some campaigners for the right to abortion, that protesters would target hospitals.

"We believe in law and order. If anyone does try to block access to termination of pregnancy, that person has to think first if it's worth the risk. We don't expect it if this is passed into law," she told Reuters.
The bill provides for a jail term of up to 10 years for anyone who obstructs a woman trying to get a legal abortion -- the same penalty which applies to backstreet abortionists.
South Africa's Medical Research Council says close to 50,000 women report to hospitals every year after botched illegal abortions from which some 425 die.
At present only about 1,000 women a year qualify for legal abortions allowed under special circumstances like incest, rape or danger to the mother's life.
The new bill provides women and girls with abortion on demand up to 12 weeks into pregnancy.

Abortion is also permitted for a further eight weeks if there is physical or emotional risk, rape, abuse or where a woman's socio-economic circumstances are significantly affected -- a clause seen by opposition parties as a loophole allowing late abortions.
The ANC's Abe Nkomo, a doctor leading the abortion review through parliament, has urged the country to welcome the reforms as a breakthrough for women's rights, saying:
"It is an important milestone in delivering choice to the women of South Africa which they have for so long been denied."

The National Party of F.W. de Klerk has threatened to lodge a constitutional challenge to the bill which party MP Sheila Camerer rejected as "a smokescreen for an immoral state programme of birth control".
The Roman Catholic Church has also taken legal advice on whether to take the bill to South Africa's highest judicial authority, the 11-judge Constitutional Court.

Abortions, which cost as little as 136 rand ($30), will be free at state hospitals and clinics for women who do not have private medical aid schemes. The first hospitals designated to carry out abortions will be identified early in the new year.
